lead: PHP control statements choose and repeat work. An if picks a branch, a loop repeats a block, and a function wraps a block under a name with its own scope. An array stores many values under keys, and foreach walks them in order. These four ideas turn a static page into server-side logic: a UPI payment page checks a status code, prints a message, and lists the last five transactions. Some syllabi call this decision making and loop controls.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for PHP syntax, dollar-prefixed variables, data types and operators.

blocks.text: An if statement runs a block when its condition is true. The condition is any expression that evaluates to true or false. elseif is tested only when the earlier conditions were false. else is the default branch and has no condition. PHP also has a short ternary form, but the full if is clearer for more than one branch.

switch compares one expression with case labels. The comparison is loose (==) by default, so "1" and 1 can match. Each case should end with break; without break, control falls through to the next case. default runs when no case matches.
PHP 8 added match. It compares with strict identity (===), returns a value, and needs no break. A match arm is value => result. If no arm matches, match throws an error unless a default arm exists.
Use decisions for validation: a form field is empty, a UPI status is "SUCCESS", or a mark crosses 40. Keep conditions simple; move a long test into a function.

sections.h3: Loops: while, do-while, for and foreach

blocks.text: while tests its condition before each pass. If the condition is false at the start, the body never runs. do-while tests after the body, so the body runs at least once. for packs init, condition and update into one line. Use for when the number of passes is known; use while when it is not.

foreach walks an array. It visits each key => value pair once, in insertion order. The loop variable is a copy; changing it does not change the array unless you write &$value. Remove the & after the loop.

break leaves the loop or switch at once. continue skips the rest of the current pass and goes to the next pass. In a for loop, continue still runs the update expression. A loop that never changes its condition is infinite; PHP stops at max_execution_time.
Example: for ($i = 1; $i <= 5; $i++) prints 1 to 5. The init runs once, the condition is checked before every pass, and the update runs after every pass.
A function is a named block. Parameters are inputs; default values make an argument optional. return sends a value back and ends the function at once. A function without return gives null.

Each function has its own scope. A variable made inside is local and disappears on return. It cannot see an outside variable unless that variable is passed as a parameter or declared global. global $x; links to the global $x. A static variable keeps its value between calls: static $count = 0; $count++.

Recursion is a function that calls itself. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the chain, and a recursive case that moves toward the base. For a positive integer n, fact(n) = n × fact(n − 1) with base fact(1) = 1. Another example is Fibonacci: fib(1) = 1, fib(2) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n − 1) + fib(n − 2). Fibonacci repeats work, so it is slower than the loop version for large n.
The figure traces fact(4) down to its base case and back up.

A PHP array is an ordered map: each value has a key. An indexed array uses keys 0, 1, 2, ...; PHP fills them when you write $a = [10, 20, 30]. An associative array uses string or integer keys you choose, such as ["name" => "Asha", "city" => "Pune"]. A multidimensional array is an array whose values are arrays; use $marks["math"][0] to reach an inner cell.

count($a) returns the number of elements. array_push($a, $x) adds $x at the end. array_keys($a) returns an array of all keys. in_array($x, $a) returns true if value $x is present. sort($a) sorts values in ascending order and resets keys; it returns true, not the sorted array.

foreach ($a as $v) gives each value. foreach ($a as $k => $v) gives each key and value. Use the key form when the key carries meaning, as in an associative array of prices. Form arrays such as $_POST come in Chapter 4.5.

spec.aria: A staircase of calls fact(4), fact(3), fact(2), fact(1); return arrows carry 1, 2, 6 and 24 back up; below, the loop output 1, 2, 6, 24, 120.

examples.question: Write a recursive PHP function fact($n) that returns n! for a positive integer n. Use a for loop to print the factorials of 1 to 5 on one line, separated by commas. Trace the call fact(4).
steps: n! means n factorial, the product 1 × 2 × ... × n. Base case: fact(1) = 1. Without it the recursion never stops.
The for loop runs $i = 1 to 5 and prints fact($i) with comma separators: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120.
examples.answer: The program prints 1, 2, 6, 24, 120; the trace of fact(4) returns 24.

code.code:
<?php
function fact($n) {
    if ($n <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return $n * fact($n - 1);
}
for ($i = 1; $i <= 5; $i++) {
    echo fact($i);
    if ($i < 5) {
        echo ", ";
    }
}
echo "\n";
?>

traps: A recursive function with no base case recurses until PHP runs out of memory or hits a stack limit. Always write and test the base case first.
A function cannot read an outside variable by default. Pass it as a parameter or declare global $name inside the function; otherwise PHP reports an undefined variable.
switch uses loose comparison and falls through without break. match uses strict ===, returns a value, and throws on no match without default.
sort($a) sorts in place and returns true. echo sort($a) prints 1, not the sorted array. Use print_r($a) or sort then print.
foreach by value gives a copy. To change elements, use foreach ($a as &$v) and unset($v) after the loop, or loop by key.

quiz.q: Which PHP loop checks its condition after the body, so the body runs at least once?
State two differences between switch and match.
quiz.a: switch uses loose comparison and needs break to avoid fall-through; match uses strict ===, returns a value, and needs no break.

quiz.q: What is printed? function f($n) { if ($n <= 1) return 1; return $n * f($n - 1); } echo f(4);
$a = [4 => 10, 9 => 20]; foreach ($a as $k => $v) { echo $k + $v; } What is the exact output?
quiz.a: 1429. First pass 4+10=14; second 9+20=29; echo joins them.

quiz.q: A function uses $count but does not receive it and does not declare it global. Explain the scope problem and one fix.
quiz.a: The function only sees local scope, so $count is undefined inside; pass $count as a parameter or declare global $count.
An indexed array of the keys: ['a','b'].

quiz.q: Why is the recursive Fibonacci function slow for large n, and what is the base case?
quiz.a: It recomputes the same subproblems many times; fib(1)=1 and fib(2)=1 stop it. Use a loop or memoization to avoid repeats.

beyond: Not for the exam. PHP 8 match expressions and named arguments reduce boilerplate in larger controllers. Generators let a foreach walk large data without building a full array. Fibers support cooperative concurrency in modern PHP. Search for PHP generators, PHP Fibers, and Xdebug recursion limits.
